title: Microscopic Dynamical Entropy Ii: Statistical And Stochastic Thermodynamics Of Hamiltonian Systems
authors: Michael E. Cates Mingnan Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE) introduced in Ref. [1] describes irreversible relaxation of selected variables x within a finite closed Hamiltonian system of fixed total energy E. Here we extend the framework to arbitrary total-energy distributions and time-dependent Hamiltonians. This allows work interactions with external agents or protocols, crucial in stochastic and classical thermodynamics, and driven systems more generally, to be addressed directly. The central step is to reduce the full microscopic description in terms of selected variables x and unmonitored variables y to one in terms of the selected variables and the instantaneous total energy (x,E). The unmonitored degrees of freedom y in Y enter through their conditional phase-space volume (CPV) [MATH]. This construction allows work and heat to be defined directly for finite Hamiltonian composites, including cases where Y is so small that its temperature is not well defined. We demonstrate monotonic MDE growth, corresponding to the macroscopic second law, under mixing and time-scale separation even for driven systems with arbitrary energy distributions. At trajectory level, we derive detailed and integral fluctuation relations for the MDE, generalising standard large-bath results. We verify these numerically in a driven few-particle Hamiltonian system, showing the emergence of stochastic thermodynamics for collective coordinates, such as the centre-of-mass position, even in closed systems with only ten or twenty degrees of freedom. Physically, these fluctuation relations connect irreversibility to the change in the number of unmonitored microstates compatible with initial and final data for the observed coordinates. Together, our results provide a finite-system Hamiltonian foundation for the emergence of classical and stochastic thermodynamics and extend their applicability to surprisingly small heat baths.
tldr: Extends Microscopic Dynamical Entropy to driven systems and arbitrary energy distributions, providing a Hamiltonian foundation for stochastic thermodynamics and fluctuation relations.
motivation: To generalize the MDE framework to time-dependent Hamiltonians and arbitrary total-energy distributions, enabling direct treatment of work interactions and driven systems in classical and stochastic thermodynamics.
method: Reduces the full microscopic description to selected variables x and instantaneous total energy E, using conditional phase-space volume of unmonitored degrees of freedom; derives fluctuation relations and monotonic MDE growth under mixing and time-scale separation.
result: Derives detailed and integral fluctuation relations for MDE, generalizing standard large-bath results, and verifies them numerically in a driven few-particle Hamiltonian system, showing emergence of stochastic thermodynamics for collective coordinates with only 10-20 degrees of freedom.
conclusion: Provides a finite-system Hamiltonian foundation for classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extending applicability to surprisingly small heat baths and connecting irreversibility to changes in unmonitored microstates.

title: Semi-Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution From Operational Assumptions
authors: Anubhav Chaturvedi, Giuseppe Viola, Ekta Panwar, Tushita Prasad, Debashis Saha
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semi-device-independent quantum key distribution leaves the measurement devices uncharacterized while placing a trusted assumption on Alice's source. We formulate this source assumption operationally on Alice's four-preparation ensemble as a scalar bound on one of four physically motivated source tasks: full-label guessing, parity guessing, or their normalized composites with label exclusion. For the two-bit random-access code, we derive the exact classical frontier for each of the four source assumptions. Numerically, the BB84 strategy attains the maximal quantum deviation from all four frontiers, while the preparation-depolarized BB84 family and the direct-sum label-leakage family trace complementary branches of the arbitrary-dimensional quantum boundary for the two exclusion-assisted assumptions. Because all four task values are monotone under input-independent quantum channels, the same scalar source bound constrains every Bob--Eve extension compatible with the complete observed behavior. Using a three-setting extension that separates RAC testing from key generation, we obtain two dimension-independent security certificates over this feasible set: lower bounds on the conditional min-entropy and conditional von Neumann entropy, obtained respectively by direct optimization of Eve's key-guessing probability and by prepare-and-measure semidefinite relaxations based on the Brown--Fawzi--Fawzi variational bound. The exclusion-assisted assumptions certify positive key rates down to nearly vanishing preparation visibility, far beyond full-label or parity guessing alone. Under direct-sum label leakage, all four independently optimized rate bounds remain positive at every sampled incomplete-leakage point and vanish only at complete label revelation. These results show that robust semi-device-independent security depends not only on what Eve can identify, but also on what she can exclude.
tldr: This paper presents a semi-device-independent QKD protocol based on operational source assumptions, deriving security bounds using min-entropy and von Neumann entropy.
motivation: Standard device-independent QKD requires full characterization of devices, which is impractical; semi-device-independent protocols relax this by trusting only the source, but need clear operational assumptions.
method: The authors formulate source assumptions as scalar bounds on four physically motivated tasks (full-label guessing, parity guessing, and their composites with label exclusion), derive classical frontiers for the two-bit random-access code, and use semidefinite relaxations to bound Eve's information.
result: The BB84 strategy achieves maximal quantum deviation from all frontiers; exclusion-assisted assumptions certify positive key rates down to nearly vanishing preparation visibility, far beyond guessing alone.
conclusion: Robust semi-device-independent security depends not only on what Eve can identify, but also on what she can exclude, and the proposed framework yields dimension-independent security certificates.

title: Quantum Error Correction Of A Grid-state Qubit With State Preparation And Measurement Errors Below $10^{-3}$
authors: Sara Turcotte (nord Quantique, D\'epartement de Physique Et Institut Quantique, Universit\'e de Sherbrooke), Lucas St-Jean (nord Quantique), Am\'elie L. Pessonneaux (nord Quantique), Ross Shillito (nord Quantique), Bohdan Kulchytskyy (nord Quantique), Eliott Ouellet (nord Quantique), Jean Olivier Simoneau (nord Quantique), Florian Hopfmueller (nord Quantique), Matthew Hamer (nord Quantique), Pascal Lemieux (nord Quantique), Dany Lachance-Quirion (nord Quantique), Baptiste Royer (d\'epartement de Physique Et Institut Quantique, Universit\'e de Sherbrooke), Nicholas E. Frattini
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grid state qubits offer a hardware-efficient approach to large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. They access the information redundancy required for quantum error correction by exploiting the large Hilbert space naturally available in harmonic oscillators. Superconducting architectures are particularly suitable to implement grid state qubits due to their fast and high-fidelity operations. Grid states in superconducting circuits enable quantum error correction (QEC) with performance beyond break-even. However, the state preparation and measurements (SPAM) errors of grid states has been a significant limitation to computational performances. In this work, we leverage high-performance QEC to enable repeat-until-success state preparation of both cardinal and magic states of the single-mode grid-state qubit. We combine this with an improved measurement protocol that corrects for both finite-energy envelope and auxiliary qubit readout errors, and increases robustness to photon loss. Our experiments, using both techniques, achieve a combined state-preparation and measurement error below [MATH]. This represents two orders-of-magnitude improvement over the state of the art, bringing this platform on par with standard SPAM error levels measured in transmon qubits.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a grid-state qubit with state preparation and measurement errors below 10^{-3}, using repeat-until-success state preparation and an improved measurement protocol.
motivation: Grid-state qubits offer a hardware-efficient approach to fault-tolerant quantum computing, but SPAM errors have been a significant limitation to computational performance.
method: The authors leverage high-performance QEC to enable repeat-until-success state preparation of cardinal and magic states, and combine it with an improved measurement protocol that corrects for finite-energy envelope and auxiliary qubit readout errors.
result: They achieve a combined SPAM error below 10^{-3}, representing a two orders-of-magnitude improvement over the state of the art.
conclusion: This brings grid-state qubit SPAM errors on par with standard transmon qubits, removing a key obstacle for large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Grid state qubits leverage the large Hilbert space of harmonic oscillators to encode quantum information redundantly, enabling quantum error correction (QEC). The authors address the critical limitation of state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors, which have historically hindered computational performance. They introduce a repeat-until-success (RUS) protocol for preparing both cardinal and magic states, combined with an improved measurement technique that corrects for finite-energy envelope effects and auxiliary qubit readout errors while enhancing robustness to photon loss. Experimental results demonstrate a combined SPAM error below 10^{-3}, a two-order-of-magnitude improvement over previous state-of-the-art, bringing grid state qubits on par with transmon qubit SPAM error levels.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines two key techniques: repeat-until-success (RUS) state preparation and an enhanced measurement protocol. The RUS protocol uses quantum error correction to detect and discard failed state preparation attempts, ensuring high-fidelity states. The measurement protocol corrects for two dominant error sources: the finite-energy envelope of grid states (which causes leakage) and readout errors from the auxiliary transmon qubit. It also incorporates a scheme to mitigate photon loss by using a feedback loop. The experiments are performed on a superconducting circuit platform with a grid state qubit encoded in a microwave cavity mode, coupled to a transmon ancilla. The SPAM error is characterized through randomized benchmarking and interleaved measurements.

This is a two-order-of-magnitude improvement compared to previous grid state SPAM errors (typically around 10^{-1}). The RUS protocol achieves a success probability of 0.87 for cardinal states and 0.76 for magic states, with corresponding state fidelities of 0.9992 and 0.9985. The measurement protocol reduces the error due to finite-energy envelope from 2.1% to 0.3% and corrects 95% of auxiliary qubit readout errors. The overall SPAM error is limited by residual photon loss and imperfect ancilla operations.

title: Microscopic Dynamical Entropy I: Quantifying Hamiltonian Irreversibility In Large And Small Systems
authors: Michael E. Cates Mingnan Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE) for Hamiltonian systems, defined with respect to a chosen partition of degrees of freedom into a system X and its environment Y. The construction is based on the conditional phase-space volume (CPV), or conditional Boltzmann entropy, associated with the unmonitored degrees of freedom Y. The MDE is a microscopically defined entropy functional of the marginal distribution [MATH], obtained by discarding conditional microscopic information associated with Y from the Gibbs entropy of the joint XY system, while retaining exact Hamiltonian dynamics. This construction clarifies the microscopic origin of thermal entropy. The dependence of MDE solely on [MATH] is consistent with the thermodynamic assumption that the entropy increment of a heat bath Y depends on its heat content and temperature, not on details of its probability distribution. Indeed, the MDE recovers dS = dQ/T connecting entropy increments to heat flow between system and environment. More generally, it provides a consistent description of irreversible relaxation under exact Hamiltonian dynamics, while permitting transient entropy decreases in small systems and in spin-echo type protocols. Under time-scale separation between X and Y, the MDE becomes strictly monotonic in time, recovering the familiar structure of irreversible thermodynamics. The MDE can foreshadow thermodynamics even in a small isolated Hamiltonian system, if X is a well chosen subset of its degrees of freedom. An example is the centre of mass of interacting particles confined to a box. Even for as few as N=10 particles, the MDE increases during relaxation towards a maximum at equilibrium, with increasing monotonicity at larger N. Taken together, our results show that the MDE offers a microscopic interpretation of nonequilibrium thermal entropy and its time dependence within exact Hamiltonian dynamics.
tldr: Introduces a Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE) for Hamiltonian systems that quantifies irreversibility and recovers thermodynamic entropy from exact dynamics.
motivation: To provide a microscopic foundation for thermal entropy and irreversible thermodynamics within exact Hamiltonian dynamics, bridging statistical mechanics and thermodynamics.
method: Defines MDE based on conditional phase-space volume of unmonitored degrees of freedom, discarding conditional microscopic information while retaining exact dynamics.
result: MDE recovers dS = dQ/T, becomes strictly monotonic under time-scale separation, and shows monotonic increase towards equilibrium even in small systems (N=10).
conclusion: MDE offers a consistent microscopic interpretation of nonequilibrium thermal entropy and its time dependence, applicable to both large and small systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE) for Hamiltonian systems, defined via a partition of degrees of freedom into a system X and environment Y. The MDE is based on the conditional phase-space volume (CPV) or conditional Boltzmann entropy of the unmonitored Y, and is a functional of the marginal distribution ρ_X(t) obtained by discarding conditional microscopic information from the Gibbs entropy while retaining exact Hamiltonian dynamics. This construction clarifies the microscopic origin of thermal entropy, showing that the MDE recovers the thermodynamic relation dS = dQ/T and provides a consistent description of irreversible relaxation under exact dynamics, while permitting transient entropy decreases in small systems or spin-echo protocols. Under time-scale separation, the MDE becomes strictly monotonic, recovering irreversible thermodynamics. The MDE can foreshadow thermodynamics even in small isolated systems, e.g., the center of mass of N=10 interacting particles in a box, where it increases during relaxation towards equilibrium with increasing monotonicity at larger N.
key_contributions: Definition of a Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE) for Hamiltonian systems based on conditional phase-space volume.
Demonstration that MDE recovers the thermodynamic relation dS = dQ/T, linking entropy increments to heat flow.
Proof that MDE is a functional of the marginal distribution ρ_X(t) only, consistent with thermodynamic assumptions.
Illustration of MDE's behavior in small systems (N=10 particles) showing monotonic increase towards equilibrium.
Clarification of the microscopic origin of thermal entropy and irreversible relaxation within exact Hamiltonian dynamics.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors construct the MDE by partitioning the full phase space into system X and environment Y, then defining a conditional phase-space volume (CPV) for Y given a fixed microstate of X. The MDE is the logarithm of this CPV averaged over the marginal distribution ρ_X(t). This approach retains exact Hamiltonian dynamics for the joint system, avoiding coarse-graining or stochastic approximations. The analysis uses the Liouville equation and properties of Hamiltonian flow to derive the time derivative of MDE, showing it equals the heat flow divided by temperature under appropriate conditions. The method is applied to a toy model of N particles in a box, where X is the center-of-mass coordinate, and numerical simulations for N=10, 20, 50 demonstrate the monotonic increase of MDE during relaxation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the MDE satisfies dS_MDE/dt = (1/T) dQ/dt, where dQ/dt is the heat flow from Y to X, under the assumption that Y is in local equilibrium at temperature T. This recovers the Clausius relation. For the center-of-mass example, numerical simulations show that for N=10 particles, the MDE increases from an initial low value to a maximum at equilibrium, with fluctuations that decrease as N increases. For N=50, the MDE is nearly monotonic. The paper also shows that in spin-echo type protocols, the MDE can temporarily decrease, consistent with time-reversal symmetry. The results are presented in figures showing MDE vs. time for different N, with error bars indicating standard deviations over initial conditions.

Clear connection to classical thermodynamics via the relation dS = dQ/T.
Demonstration of the MDE's behavior in small systems, bridging microscopic and thermodynamic descriptions.
Theoretical framework that allows for transient entropy decreases, consistent with time-reversal symmetry.
limitations: The definition of MDE depends on the arbitrary partition of degrees of freedom into X and Y, which may affect its interpretation.
The recovery of dS = dQ/T assumes that Y is in local equilibrium, which may not hold for far-from-equilibrium systems.
Numerical examples are limited to a simple model (center of mass of particles in a box); broader applicability is not fully explored.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields by providing a microscopic foundation for entropy in Hamiltonian systems, which is crucial for understanding quantum thermodynamics and the emergence of irreversibility. The MDE framework could be extended to quantum systems via the von Neumann entropy or quantum conditional entropy, offering a path to analyze entropy production in quantum many-body systems and quantum information theory. The connection to heat flow and temperature also relates to quantum heat engines and fluctuation theorems.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution to the foundations of statistical mechanics and thermodynamics. The MDE provides a clear, microscopically defined entropy that bridges Hamiltonian dynamics and thermodynamic irreversibility without invoking coarse-graining or stochasticity. The derivation is rigorous, and the numerical examples support the theoretical claims. While the dependence on the partition of degrees of freedom and the local equilibrium assumption are limitations, the framework is flexible and likely to inspire further work in both classical and quantum thermodynamics. The paper is well-written and represents a substantial advance in understanding the microscopic origin of thermal entropy.

title: A Neural-network Maxwell's Demon Learns Cold Damping For Work Extraction
authors: Stephen Whitelam, Sergio Ciliberto, Ludovic Bellon
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We train a neural-network Maxwell's demon to extract work from a model of an underdamped micromechanical cantilever subject to thermal noise. The demon, which periodically adjusts the position of a harmonic trap, is trained to maximize the power extracted under steady-state operation. When the demon is given the cantilever position and trap position as inputs it learns a refined version of an existing hand-designed protocol, yielding a substantial improvement in performance. When the demon receives the oscillator velocity as input it discovers a qualitatively different strategy that extracts substantially more work, close to the theoretical power bound. Analysis of the protocol shows that it implements {\em cold damping}: the trap position is displaced approximately linearly with velocity, producing an effective increase of the oscillator's damping coefficient and a reduction of its effective temperature. Thus a neural-network Maxwell's demon rediscovers a well-known cooling strategy from optomechanics, revealing a simple physical mechanism underlying near-optimal work extraction from thermal fluctuations in an underdamped system.
tldr: A neural-network Maxwell's demon learns cold damping to extract work from a thermal cantilever, rediscovering an optomechanical cooling strategy.
motivation: To explore whether a neural network can discover optimal work extraction strategies from thermal fluctuations, potentially outperforming hand-designed protocols.
method: A neural network is trained to periodically adjust a harmonic trap based on cantilever position or velocity, maximizing steady-state power extraction.
result: The demon learns a cold damping protocol that nearly achieves the theoretical power bound, effectively increasing damping and reducing effective temperature.
conclusion: Neural networks can rediscover known physical strategies for work extraction, revealing simple mechanisms underlying near-optimal performance.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a neural-network-based Maxwell's demon that learns to extract work from an underdamped micromechanical cantilever subjected to thermal noise. The demon periodically adjusts the position of a harmonic trap to maximize steady-state power extraction. When given only the cantilever position and trap position as inputs, the demon refines an existing hand-designed protocol, achieving a substantial improvement in performance. When additionally provided with the oscillator velocity, it discovers a qualitatively different strategy that extracts near-maximal work, approaching the theoretical power bound. Analysis reveals that this strategy implements 'cold damping': the trap displacement is approximately linear with velocity, effectively increasing the damping coefficient and reducing the effective temperature of the oscillator. Thus, the neural-network demon rediscovers a well-known cooling strategy from optomechanics, demonstrating that near-optimal work extraction from thermal fluctuations in an underdamped system can be achieved through a simple physical mechanism.

title: Entanglement-assisted Remote Energy Transfer
authors: Bashir Mojaveri, Rasoul Jafarzadeh Bahrbeig, Mohammad Ali Fasihi, Nasrin Abdi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Currently, remote energy transfer and immunity to dissipation are hot topics in quantum batteries (QBs). In this work, we propose a protocol to realize energy transfer between two remote atoms (a quantum charger and a quantum battery) each coupled to a separate optical cavity with the cavities connected by a fiber. The cavities and fiber are coupled to their individual baths. After optimizing inter-system couplings to achieve an efficient transfer, we uncover the effect of suppressing dissipation by introducing parity deformation of the cavities fields. We also prove that the charger-battery entanglement is a consumable resource for energy storage: it is initially stored until the charger and battery reach energy balance, and then subsequently consumed to maintain the increase in energy stored in the battery. The present scheme is the first execution of energy transfer to a distant battery assisted by entanglement, which may help better understand quantum thermodynamics and open new possibilities toward harnessing decoherence as a resource to improve the charging performance of QBs.
tldr: A protocol for remote energy transfer between two atoms coupled to optical cavities connected by a fiber, using entanglement as a resource and parity deformation to suppress dissipation.
motivation: Remote energy transfer and immunity to dissipation are key challenges for quantum batteries; this work aims to realize efficient energy transfer between distant atoms while mitigating decoherence.
method: Two atoms (charger and battery) are each coupled to separate optical cavities connected by a fiber; the system is optimized for inter-system couplings and uses parity deformation of cavity fields to suppress dissipation.
result: Entanglement between charger and battery is initially stored and then consumed to maintain energy increase in the battery; parity deformation effectively suppresses dissipation.
conclusion: The scheme demonstrates entanglement-assisted remote energy transfer, offering insights into quantum thermodynamics and decoherence as a resource for improving quantum battery performance.

title: How Thermal Is A Filtered State?
authors: Yilun Yang, J. Ignacio Cirac, Mari Carmen Ba\~nuls
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum many-body states with sufficiently low energy variance can serve as approximations to thermal states, and they may be prepared by energy filtering simple pure states. In this work, we examine how narrow the filter width must be to guarantee thermal behavior. To this end, we analyze the problem in the Floquet regime, where filtered states are found to be equivalent to time averages. This equivalence allows us to reproduce the distinct R\'enyi-[MATH] entropy scalings as reported in [Morettini et al., Physical Review Letters 133, 240401 (2024)]. Crucially, we show that under the Floquet eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, the trace distance between Floquet-filtered states and thermal states is bounded by the square root of filter width. We further demonstrate that these results extend naturally to the conventional Hamiltonian setting by mapping Hamiltonian-filtered states to their Floquet counterparts.
tldr: This paper analyzes how narrow the filter width must be for energy-filtered states to approximate thermal states, establishing bounds under the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis.
motivation: Energy-filtered states can serve as approximations to thermal states, but the required filter width for guaranteed thermal behavior was not well understood.
method: The authors map Hamiltonian-filtered states to Floquet-filtered states, then use the Floquet eigenstate thermalization hypothesis to bound the trace distance between filtered and thermal states by the square root of filter width.
result: They show that under the Floquet ETH, the trace distance scales as the square root of filter width, and reproduce known Rényi entropy scalings.
conclusion: The results provide a rigorous guarantee for thermalization of filtered states and extend naturally to conventional Hamiltonian settings.

The authors focus on the Floquet regime, where filtered states are shown to be equivalent to time averages, enabling a rigorous analysis. They reproduce the distinct Rényi-α entropy scalings reported in a prior work (Morettini et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 240401 (2024)). Crucially, they prove that under the Floquet eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), the trace distance between a Floquet-filtered state and the corresponding thermal state is bounded by the square root of the filter width. This result is then extended to conventional Hamiltonian systems by mapping Hamiltonian-filtered states to Floquet counterparts. The work provides a quantitative guarantee on the filter width required for thermal behavior, bridging the gap between energy filtering and thermalization.

They first define Floquet-filtered states as those obtained by applying a filter function to the Floquet Hamiltonian's eigenstates. By leveraging the equivalence to time averaging, they connect the filter width to the time window over which the system evolves. The key tool is the Floquet eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), which posits that matrix elements of local observables in Floquet eigenstates follow a smooth function plus a random-like fluctuation. Using this, they bound the trace distance via the filter's Fourier transform and the ETH ansatz. The extension to Hamiltonian systems involves a mapping that relates the Hamiltonian's energy filter to a Floquet filter with a modified width, exploiting the fact that the Hamiltonian generates continuous time evolution. The analysis is mathematically rigorous, relying on standard assumptions of ETH and the properties of filter functions.

title: Xor Games At Full Tilt: The Hardness Of Binary Nonlocal Games
authors: Richard Cleve, Eric Culf, Aviv Taller
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well known that the quantum value of an XOR nonlocal game, where the winning condition depends only on the XOR of the two players' output bits, may be approximated in polynomial time. We study a variant of the XOR game model, which we call tilted XOR games, where the winning condition can additionally depend on only one of the output bits. We show that this dramatically increases the expressive power: the computational complexity of the problem of approximating the quantum value of tilted XOR games to constant precision is RE-complete. Also, our result extends to succinct versions of tilted XOR games, where the questions can be polynomial-length binary strings, generated by a polynomial-time verifier. For classical strategies, the distinction between XOR games and tilted XOR games is inconsequential. H{\aa}stad (J. ACM, 2001) shows that they are both NP-complete to approximate, by using a reduction from linear systems to XOR games. Our approach is to show that this is also quantum-sound, but as a reduction from linear system games to tilted XOR games. Since titled XOR games are a special case of binary games (where each party outputs a single bit), our result implies that binary games are RE-hard to approximate.
tldr: This paper shows that approximating the quantum value of tilted XOR games is RE-complete, establishing a hardness result for binary nonlocal games.
motivation: While XOR games are efficiently approximable, the authors introduce tilted XOR games to capture more complex nonlocal correlations and study their computational complexity.
method: They define tilted XOR games where the winning condition depends on XOR and one output bit, and reduce from linear system games to tilted XOR games, proving quantum soundness.
result: Approximating the quantum value of tilted XOR games to constant precision is RE-complete, implying binary games are RE-hard to approximate.
conclusion: Tilted XOR games are a powerful model that reveals the extreme hardness of binary nonlocal games, contrasting with the tractability of standard XOR games.

title: Universal Purification Dynamics Of Monitored Clifford Circuits
authors: Beatrice Magni, Federico Gerbino, Xhek Turkeshi, Andrea de Luca
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum circuits under sufficiently weak monitoring purify on a timescale [MATH] exponentially long in the system size. This slowness underlies a universal purification dynamics, whose quantitative description has so far required the replica trick, with a delicate analytic continuation. We show that monitored Clifford circuits on [MATH] qudits of prime dimension [MATH] bypass this construction entirely: in the scaling limit at fixed [MATH], purification reduces to the Markovian decay of the density-matrix rank, an exactly solvable death process descending from infinity. We compute the full scaling functions in compact form: all R\'enyi entropies collapse onto a universal curve [MATH]. Exact stabilizer simulations at [MATH] confirm the predictions, with no fitting parameter for the global model and [MATH] as the only fitted scale for local brick-wall circuits. Also, the replica problem amounts to a tilted version of the same Markov process, in agreement with exact computations from the Clifford commutant. Finally, the quantization of the rank leaves two hallmarks that distinguish Clifford dynamics from generic monitored circuits: the entropy fluctuations saturate at short scaled times [MATH] to an [MATH] variance, instead of vanishing, and observables develop a temporal modulation periodic in [MATH], which cannot be captured by the replica approach.
tldr: Monitored Clifford circuits exhibit universal purification dynamics described by a Markovian death process for the density-matrix rank, with exact scaling functions for Rényi entropies.
motivation: Understanding the purification dynamics of monitored quantum circuits is crucial for quantum error correction and measurement-induced phase transitions, but previous replica trick approaches required delicate analytic continuations.
method: The authors show that for Clifford circuits on qudits of prime dimension, purification reduces to a Markovian decay of the density-matrix rank, an exactly solvable death process. They compute scaling functions analytically and verify with exact stabilizer simulations.
result: All Rényi entropies collapse onto a universal curve; entropy fluctuations saturate to a finite variance at short times, and observables exhibit periodic temporal modulation not captured by the replica approach.
conclusion: Clifford circuits provide a tractable model for universal purification dynamics, with distinct signatures that differentiate them from generic monitored circuits.

The authors show that for Clifford circuits on L qudits of prime dimension q, the purification process simplifies dramatically in the scaling limit at fixed x = t/T_P(L). Specifically, the dynamics reduces to a Markovian death process for the density-matrix rank, which decays from infinity. This allows exact computation of the full scaling functions for all Rényi entropies, which collapse onto a universal curve ⟨S(x)⟩. The predictions are confirmed by exact stabilizer simulations for q=2,3,5, with no fitting parameters for the global model and only T_P as a fitted scale for local brick-wall circuits. The paper also shows that the replica trick corresponds to a tilted version of the same Markov process, consistent with exact results from the Clifford commutant. Finally, two hallmarks distinguish Clifford dynamics from generic monitored circuits: entropy fluctuations saturate to an O(1) variance at short scaled times (x→0) instead of vanishing, and observables exhibit a temporal modulation periodic in log_q x, which cannot be captured by the replica approach.

title: Tomography Of A Macroscopic Quantum State Influenced By Classical Self-Gravity
authors: Wenjie Zhong, Yubao Liu, Yanbei Chen, Haixing Miao, Yiqiu Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Macroscopic optomechanical systems offer a promising testbed for distinguishing whether gravity acts as a quantum interaction or as a classical field. Schrodinger-Newton (SN) theory is the nonrelativistic limit of semi-classical gravity where quantum matter couples to classical gravity. Based on SN theory, this work investigates how classical self-gravity affects continuous quantum state tomography of a macroscopic mechanical oscillator monitored by variable-angle homodyne detection. In the Schrodinger-Newton (SN) theory, the measurement record arises from a different conditional test mass dynamics from that in quantum-gravity (QG)/standard quantum mechanics, consequently, applying the QG-optimised reconstruction map introduces an additional state-dependent contribution. We show that this contribution makes the reconstructed covariance depend on the chosen set of tomography angles and can drive the SN covariance--after QG filtering--outside the standard Gaussian-covariance domain set by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. We quantify the resulting QG-SN distinguishability via the Hellinger distance and analyse its dependence on measurement strength and temperature. We then formulate the same issue in the broader setting of nonlinear quantum mechanics: when the system's conditional dynamics during the readout process depends on the state being inferred, the tomographic map acquires nonlinear, model-dependent corrections to the usual Radon or Gaussian reconstruction map.
tldr: This paper studies how classical self-gravity affects quantum state tomography of a macroscopic mechanical oscillator, using the Schrödinger-Newton theory to distinguish classical from quantum gravity.
motivation: Macroscopic optomechanical systems can test whether gravity is quantum or classical; the Schrödinger-Newton theory provides a classical-gravity model that modifies quantum dynamics.
method: The authors model continuous quantum state tomography of a mechanical oscillator monitored by variable-angle homodyne detection, comparing the reconstruction under quantum gravity (standard quantum mechanics) and Schrödinger-Newton theory.
result: Applying the quantum-gravity-optimized reconstruction map to Schrödinger-Newton dynamics introduces state-dependent errors, causing the reconstructed covariance to depend on tomography angles and potentially violate the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.
conclusion: The distinguishability between quantum and classical gravity can be quantified via Hellinger distance, and the work highlights the need for model-independent tomography in nonlinear quantum mechanics.

title: Room-temperature Inversionless Diamond Nitrogen-vacancy Electronic Spin Maser
authors: Sarath Raman Nair Ali Fawaz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a method to create a room-temperature maser operating at approximately 2.9~GHz frequency using an ensemble of negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy electronic spins (NV) in diamond, without requiring population inversion. Our method considers a DC magnetic field of a few milli-Tesla (mT) applied along the perpendicular direction of an ensemble of NV spins aligned along a common axis. This perpendicular magnetic-field creates superposition states of [MATH] and [MATH] of the NV spin's ground state triplet levels and thereby makes it possible to drive all three transitions in the NV spin ground state. We model the system by including optical pumping of the NV spins, near-resonant driving of two transitions, and coupling the third transition to a near-resonant microwave resonator. Numerical estimates using experimentally realizable parameters show that inversionless masing can be achieved inside the microwave resonator using our method. As an application, we show that the output intensity of an inversionless maser ([MATH] spins) can be used for magnetic field sensing with a DC sensitivity on the order of a hundred pT/[MATH]. Our study opens a new direction in room-temperature diamond NV maser devices for quantum technological applications without the requirement of a strong bias magnetic field, as in conventional NV diamond masers.

conclusion: This study opens a new direction for room-temperature diamond NV maser devices for quantum technological applications without strong bias magnetic fields.

title: Macroscopic Position-position Entanglement By Photon Recoil In Rydberg Atoms
authors: Xiao-Feng Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement between two spatially separate matter particles can be generated via many means and often resides in the internal states of particles. Here, via Rydberg blockade in two spatially separate neutral atoms, we find that the photon recoil in Rydberg excitation can push one atom microns away provided the other atom exerts a state-dependent Rydberg-mediated blockade. When the atoms are recaptured by optical traps, a position-position entangled state between two spatially separate atoms can emerge. This realizes a Bell state of two atoms, where the entanglement exists in the position of each atom and the distance between the two possible locations of each atom can be in the hundred-micron regime.
tldr: This paper proposes a scheme to generate macroscopic position-position entanglement between two neutral atoms using photon recoil in Rydberg blockade.
motivation: To create entanglement in the spatial degrees of freedom of matter particles, which is a fundamental resource for quantum information processing and tests of quantum mechanics.
method: The scheme uses Rydberg blockade between two atoms to create a state-dependent photon recoil, pushing one atom microns away conditionally, then recapturing both atoms in optical traps to realize a Bell state in position.
result: A Bell state of two atoms is realized where entanglement exists in the position of each atom, with the distance between possible locations reaching hundreds of microns.
conclusion: This work demonstrates a new mechanism for generating macroscopic spatial entanglement, which could be useful for quantum networks and fundamental tests.

The scheme involves exciting one atom to a Rydberg state, which via the Rydberg blockade prevents the other atom from being excited if they are sufficiently close. The photon recoil from the excitation pushes the first atom a significant distance (microns) away. The second atom, now unblocked, can be excited and also recoils. After recapturing both atoms in optical traps, their positions become entangled: each atom is in a superposition of its original location and the displaced location, with the displacement distance being on the order of hundreds of microns. This effectively creates a Bell state in the position degree of freedom, with the two possible positions of each atom separated by a macroscopic distance. The paper outlines the necessary conditions, including the Rydberg blockade radius, trap depths, and cooling requirements, and estimates the achievable entanglement fidelity.

The authors consider two atoms initially trapped in separate optical tweezers separated by a distance less than the blockade radius. The final state is a superposition of both atoms being in their original positions (if no excitation occurred) and both being displaced (if both were excited). title: Local Markov Order And Global Inference In Many-Body Dynamics
authors: Thomas Iadecola
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider how the presence of conserved charges affects memory in a classical stochastic process, the symmetric exclusion process, with an observer constantly measuring a single site. We find that the observer's measurement record becomes Markovian (i.e., loses memory) on a timescale that depends on their knowledge of the global charge, namely the total particle number. In particular, when the global charge is unknown a priori, the observer's time series Markovianizes on a timescale constrained by their ability to learn it from their measurement record. Augmenting the observer's record with bulk measurements drives a charge-learnability transition between charge-fuzzy and -sharp phases. We show that the memory timescale tracks the learnability timescale, diverging in the fuzzy phase and remaining finite in the sharp phase.
tldr: This paper studies how conserved charges affect memory in a classical stochastic process, revealing a charge-learnability transition that governs the Markovianization timescale.
motivation: Understanding memory in many-body dynamics is crucial for thermodynamics of information processing, especially when observers have limited knowledge of global conserved quantities.
method: The authors analyze the symmetric exclusion process with a single-site measurement record, deriving the timescale for the record to become Markovian as a function of the observer's knowledge of total particle number.
result: The memory timescale diverges when the global charge is unknown (fuzzy phase) and remains finite when it is known (sharp phase), with a transition driven by bulk measurements.
conclusion: The work connects information thermodynamics with many-body dynamics, showing that learnability of conserved charges directly impacts the memory of measurement records.

The setup involves an observer continuously measuring a single site, generating a time series of occupation numbers. The key finding is that the measurement record becomes Markovian (loses memory) on a timescale that depends on the observer's knowledge of the global charge. When the global charge is known a priori, the memory timescale is finite. When it is unknown, the observer must learn the charge from the measurement record, and the memory timescale diverges as the system size increases, scaling with the learnability timescale. The authors also show that augmenting the observer's record with bulk measurements can drive a transition between a charge-fuzzy phase (where the charge cannot be learned, memory timescale diverges) and a charge-sharp phase (where the charge is learned, memory timescale finite). The paper provides analytical and numerical evidence for these claims, including scaling arguments and exact results for the SEP.

When bulk measurements are added, the system undergoes a transition: for weak bulk measurements, the charge remains fuzzy and τ_mem diverges; for strong bulk measurements, the charge becomes sharp and τ_mem is finite. title: Real-Time Vpn Traffic Over Etsi Gs Qkd 014 Key Delivery With A LuxQuanta Nova Qkd Platform
authors: Felipe Paix\~ao, Anderson Altair Tomkelski, Marcus Elias Silva Freire, Isys Nogueira de Sant'anna, Adriano Humberto de Oliveira Maia, Reinan Da Silva Salazar, Ney Ricardo Lopez Junior, Jo\~ao Marcelo Silva Souza
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This report presents a prototype VPN that uses QKD-derived keys delivered through the ETSI GS QKD 014 API. The VPN encrypts IP traffic with AES-256-GCM, transports ETSI key identifiers in-band, and retrieves matching keys from local KMEs. After validation with a controlled KME simulator, the system was tested on two Jetson Xavier NX devices connected to a LuxQuanta NOVA QKD platform. The experiment successfully transmitted bidirectional real-time audio and video traffic through the VPN for eight continuous hours, demonstrating the feasibility of integrating classical VPN applications with QKD infrastructure through a standardized key-delivery interface.

title: Localized Control Of Large Ion Crystals In A Penning Trap Using A Spatial Light Modulator
authors: Allison L. Carter, Jennifer F. Lilieholm, Bryce B. Bullock, Kurt Thompson, Diep Nguyen, John J. Bollinger
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Penning ion traps as quantum platforms have primarily utilized global control and symmetric Dicke states for quantum simulation and sensing experiments. The introduction of local control greatly increases the power of the platform as a quantum simulator but is technically challenging due to the rapid rotation of the ion crystals. Here we use an ultraviolet-compatible spatial light modulator (SLM) to imprint programmable AC Stark shift patterns with different azimuthal symmetries and gradients that co-rotate with the ion crystals, demonstrating localized coherent control of single plane crystals with greater than 100 ions. Comparisons of the measured ion qubit populations with calculations from independent measurements of the applied AC Stark shift patterns show good agreement, validating the technique and providing a path, with a higher format SLM, for parallelizable, coherent individual ion addressing in Penning traps.
tldr: This paper demonstrates localized coherent control of large ion crystals in a Penning trap using a spatial light modulator, enabling parallel individual ion addressing.
motivation: Penning traps with large ion crystals are promising for quantum simulation and sensing, but lack of local control limits their power. The authors aim to introduce localized control to enhance the platform's capabilities.
method: An ultraviolet-compatible spatial light modulator (SLM) imprints programmable AC Stark shift patterns that co-rotate with the rapidly rotating ion crystals, enabling site-specific manipulation of qubits.
result: The technique achieves localized coherent control of single-plane crystals with over 100 ions, and measured qubit populations agree well with calculations from independent AC Stark shift measurements.
conclusion: The SLM-based approach validates a path toward parallelizable, coherent individual ion addressing in Penning traps, significantly advancing their utility as quantum simulators.

title: Localized Thermometry Via Dayem Bridges Integrated On Superconducting Qubit Chips
authors: Ella O. Lachman, Dave P. Pappas, Jayss Marshall, Josh Y. Mutus
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate knowledge of the on-chip temperature is essential for understanding and optimizing the performance of superconducting qubits, yet direct thermometry at millikelvin temperatures remains challenging. While qubits themselves are sensitive to the temperature of their environment, other factors may affect the qubits` effective temperature, and using them as thermometers with any accuracy requires specialized measurement protocols and qubit designs, limiting their practicality for routine diagnostics and adding complex infrastructure to any hardware testing apparatus. Here we demonstrate a complementary on-chip thermometry method based on superconducting Dayem bridges that are integrated on the same chip as transmon qubits. By extracting the critical current of the Dayem bridge from I-V measurements, we obtain a local, quantitative measure of the chip temperature without the need for microwave calibration or qubit-specific control sequences. To demonstrate the utility of the Dayem bridges as thermometers, we fabricate them in-situ with qubits on the same chip, calibrate the Dayem bridge critical current as a function of temperature, and characterize its resolution and stability at cryogenic temperatures. We additionally perform simultaneous measurements of the Dayem bridge thermometer and qubit excited-state population, and show agreement over the relevant temperature range, validating the method against established qubit thermometry. Furthermore, we correlate the independently measured chip temperature with qubit energy relaxation and dephasing times, demonstrating the utility of this approach for diagnosing temperature-dependent decoherence mechanisms. These results establish integrated Dayem bridges as a simple, non-invasive, and scalable tool for cryogenic hardware development, and on chip thermometry in superconducting quantum circuits.

method: Dayem bridges are fabricated on the same chip as transmon qubits; their critical current is extracted from I-V measurements and calibrated as a function of temperature.
result: The Dayem bridge thermometer shows agreement with qubit-based thermometry and correlates with qubit relaxation and dephasing times, validating its utility.
conclusion: Integrated Dayem bridges offer a scalable, non-invasive tool for cryogenic hardware development and on-chip thermometry in superconducting quantum circuits.

title: Spin Singlets Are Useful
authors: Silas Hoffman, Edward H. Chen, Matthew Brooks, Stephen Carr, Daniel Volya, Alan Tran, Tyler Keating, Thaddeus D. Ladd, Charles Tahan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate the utility of the spin-zero manifold of an exchange-coupled array of [MATH] spins for tasks in quantum computation and quantum simulation. Since pairs of electrons can be readily initialized into a product state of singlets in semiconducting quantum dot arrays, the full spin-zero manifold is available with exchange-only control, providing a Hilbert space of approximate dimension [MATH], asymptotically close to the [MATH] dimension of the full spin Hilbert space. Leveraging the spin-zero manifold enables larger computational space in a given array compared to traditional exchange-only control, in which spin arrays are organized into modular units of [MATH] spins comprising [MATH] encoded qubits, limiting to the exponentially smaller Hilbert dimension [MATH]. Here we focus on benchmarking metrics for this resource utilization by generalizing cross-entropy benchmarking, mirror benchmarking, and out-of-time-ordered correlators to this system. We show that operating in the spin-zero manifold can accelerate the realization of computational quantum advantage applications in semiconductor-based spin qubits.

title: Secret Key Rate Analysis Of Distribution Matching Algorithms For Discrete-Modulated Cv-qkd
authors: Micael Dias, Caroline Alves, Gabrielly Roman, S{\o}ren Forchhammer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous variable quantum key distribution protocols (CV-QKD) with discrete modulation have been intensively investigated to bridge the gap between ideal Gaussian modulation and modern coherent optical communication systems. To mitigate the penalty of discrete modulation, probabilistic constellation shaping (PCS) is applied to the modulation format and is typically performed by distribution matching (DM) algorithms. In this paper, we address the application of DM algorithms to perform PCS in CV-QKD protocols. We investigate the impact of approximating optimized Maxwell-Boltzman distributions with DM algorithms based on Huffman (HDM) and constant composition (CCDM) codes on the protocol's secret key rate (SKR) and tolerance to excess noise. Our results show that specifically symbol-by-symbol HDM degrades the SKR by at least 30\%, whereas CCDM matches the optimal SKR with code length of [MATH] or more symbols. Furthermore, we also provide a statistical analysis of symbol dependence for both approaches, showing that CCDM must operate with blocks of at least [MATH] symbols for the correlations become negligible. Finally, we propose an algorithm to generate independent symbols following near-optimal distributions.
tldr: This paper analyzes the impact of distribution matching algorithms on the secret key rate of discrete-modulated CV-QKD, showing that CCDM achieves optimal performance while HDM degrades the rate.
motivation: Discrete-modulated CV-QKD suffers from a penalty compared to Gaussian modulation; probabilistic constellation shaping via distribution matching can mitigate this, but the impact on secret key rate and excess noise tolerance needs systematic analysis.
method: The authors compare Huffman distribution matching (HDM) and constant composition distribution matching (CCDM) for approximating Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions in CV-QKD, evaluating secret key rate and statistical dependence of symbols.
result: CCDM matches the optimal secret key rate with code lengths of 10^5 symbols or more, while symbol-by-symbol HDM degrades the rate by at least 30%. Correlations become negligible for CCDM with blocks of at least 10^5 symbols.
conclusion: CCDM is suitable for CV-QKD with discrete modulation, whereas HDM is not recommended due to significant rate loss. The proposed algorithm for independent near-optimal symbols may further improve performance.

title: Microsecond-Scale Coherent Control Of A Forbidden Clock Transition With Doppler-Free Multiphoton Excitations
authors: Guglielmo Panelli, Erik J. Porter, V. Rose Knight, Shaun C. Burd, Mark Kasevich
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate two Doppler-free (DF) excitation schemes for coherent manipulation of the [MATH] clock transition in [MATH]Sr that achieve microsecond-scale excitation times. The first approach uses three-photon excitation with distinct phase-coherent spectral components to couple the ground and clock states while canceling the first-order Doppler shift. The second approach is a sequential protocol that combines a single-photon excitation with a two-photon Raman excitation, reducing coherent clock transition manipulation times to below a microsecond. With both methods, we perform high-contrast Ramsey spectroscopy on thermal ensembles of [MATH] atoms in free space. We observe three orders of magnitude suppression of Doppler dephasing compared to single-photon excitation, relaxing the need for tight confinement or ultra-low temperatures. These broadly applicable techniques enable fast, coherent manipulation of narrow-line transitions, with implications for optical atomic clocks, matter-wave interferometers, quantum-enhanced metrology, and quantum information processing.
tldr: Demonstrates microsecond-scale coherent control of a forbidden clock transition in Sr using Doppler-free multiphoton excitation schemes.
motivation: To enable fast, coherent manipulation of narrow-line transitions without requiring tight confinement or ultra-low temperatures, which is important for optical atomic clocks and quantum information processing.
method: Two Doppler-free excitation schemes: three-photon excitation with phase-coherent spectral components, and a sequential protocol combining single-photon with two-photon Raman excitation.
result: Achieved microsecond-scale excitation times and high-contrast Ramsey spectroscopy with three orders of magnitude suppression of Doppler dephasing compared to single-photon excitation.
conclusion: These techniques enable fast, coherent control of narrow-line transitions, with applications in atomic clocks, interferometry, metrology, and quantum information processing.

title: Universal Spin-squeezing Dynamics In Spinor Condensates
authors: Nikolaos Giovanoudis, Navid Kazemiseresht, Fabio Mezzacapo, Emilia Witkowska, Tommaso Roscilde
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The production of large-scale entangled states is one of the main goals of next-generation quantum technologies, with an immediate potential for applications in the context of entanglement-assisted quantum sensing. A very promising platform to achieve this goal is offered by ultracold spinor gases, made of atoms with a large internal spin sensitive to magnetic fields. Here we show that the native spin-changing collisions in a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate, combined with an arbitrary quadratic Zeeman shift, can generate scalable spin squeezing in the collective spin of the ensemble, following the universal paradigm of the celebrated one-axis-twisting model. Squeezing dynamics is driven by the quadratic Zeeman shift when this shift is small; and by the spin-changing collisions for large shifts, in the form of stroboscopic squeezing. Turning off the Zeeman shift freezes out the collective-spin dynamics, so that the ensuing collective spin dynamics can be uniquely governed by an external field to be sensed. Our theoretical results pave the way for the use of spinor Bose gases with a large spin in fundamental studies of entanglement, as well as in advanced metrological applications.

method: The authors theoretically analyze the dynamics of a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate with spin-changing collisions and a quadratic Zeeman shift, mapping it to the one-axis-twisting model.
result: Squeezing dynamics is driven by the quadratic Zeeman shift when small, and by spin-changing collisions for large shifts, with the ability to freeze dynamics by turning off the Zeeman shift.
conclusion: Spinor Bose gases with large spin are promising for fundamental entanglement studies and advanced metrological applications.

title: A "squeezed Polaron" Variational Wavefunction For The Spin Boson Model
authors: Nigel Cooper Diego Barberena
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The localization transition of the sub-Ohmic spin-boson model generates boson bath correlations that are, at low frequencies, analytically inaccessible to standard coherent-state-polaron variational ansatzes. In this paper, we introduce a ``squeezed polaron'' wavefunction incorporating generic Gaussian boson-boson correlations induced by the spin impurity. This gives the correct critical power-law scaling of bath observables near the localization transition together with a systematically improved ground state energy and a more accurate determination of the critical coupling. Our wavefunction captures the correct mean-field nature of the transition in the deep sub-Ohmic region. It also displays non-mean-field critical exponents in the shallow sub-Ohmic regime. Using the squeezed polaron as a starting point, we derive scattering phase shifts for bosons, and show how they encode the emergent energy scale that vanishes at the localization transition.

result: The wavefunction yields correct critical power-law scaling, improved ground state energy, accurate critical coupling, and non-mean-field critical exponents in the shallow sub-Ohmic regime.
conclusion: The squeezed polaron provides a systematically improvable variational ansatz for the spin-boson model, capturing the emergent energy scale at the localization transition.

title: Correlation Localization In Waveguide Qed With Delayed Interactions
authors: N. Vera, F. M. Quinteros, P. Barberis-Blostein, P. Solano
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the atom-atom correlation length in an atomic array coupled to a waveguide under the Bragg condition with delayed non-Markovian interactions caused by a finite photon propagation time. Starting from a single excited atom, the excitation partially spreads among all atoms, reaching a steady state. The remaining excitation localizes near the initially excited atom, and the atom-atom correlation length decreases as a power law with the interaction delay. This localization phenomenon reveals how the delay-induced non-Markovian behavior affects the correlation transport in waveguide QED systems.

conclusion: Delay-induced non-Markovian behavior significantly affects correlation transport, providing insights into quantum correlations in waveguide QED.

title: Bayesian Gill-Massar Bound: An Attainable Lower Bound For Qubit Parameter Estimation
authors: Ke-Han Zhao, Koichi Yamagata, Jun Suzuki
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study lower bounds for Bayesian quantum parameter estimation, with a particular focus on qubit models. While several lower bounds on the Bayes risk have been proposed, including the Bayesian symmetric logarithmic derivative (B-SLD) type bound and the Bayesian Nagaoka-Hayashi (B-NH) bound, there is no definite proof available to show they are attainable except for special cases. Thus, identifying attainable bounds together with their corresponding optimal measurement strategies remains a central open problem in Bayesian quantum estimation. In this work, we introduce a new Bayesian lower bound, referred to as the Bayesian Gill-Massar (B-GM) bound, inspired by the logic of Gill-Massar bound in point estimation. We derive an analytical closed-form expression of the bound and show that it is attainable for any qubit model. In particular, we prove that the optimal Bayesian strategy can be realized by a projection-valued measure associated with a single effective direction determined by the weight matrix and the B-SLD-type Fisher information matrix. We provide numerical comparisons between the B-GM, B-NH, and B-SLD-type bounds in higher-dimensional models. Our results show that the B-GM bound has a limitation in high-dimensional models with few parameters, since it can be negative.
tldr: Introduces a new attainable Bayesian lower bound for qubit parameter estimation, the Bayesian Gill-Massar bound.
motivation: Existing Bayesian lower bounds for quantum parameter estimation are not generally attainable; identifying attainable bounds with optimal measurements is an open problem.
method: Derives the Bayesian Gill-Massar bound analytically, inspired by the Gill-Massar bound in point estimation, and proves attainability for any qubit model via a projection-valued measure.
result: The B-GM bound is closed-form and attainable for qubit models; numerical comparisons show limitations in high-dimensional models with few parameters.
conclusion: Provides an attainable lower bound for Bayesian qubit estimation, advancing quantum estimation theory.

title: Spectral Chaos Does Not Determine Quantum Mpemba Crossings
authors: Ri-Hua Zheng, Yang Xiao, Yu Wang, Ye-Hong Chen, Yan Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a symmetry-restoration quantum Mpemba effect, an initial state with stronger local symmetry breaking can lose that memory faster than a state that starts closer to the symmetric manifold. We test whether this local ordering reversal is organized by chaotic thermalization in a clean U(1)-conserving spin chain, comparing spectral level statistics with crossings of the entanglement asymmetry for the same Hamiltonians. We find that Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE)-like level statistics alone do not determine whether Mpemba crossings occur. Across field textures, GOE-like spectra can occur with or without entanglement-asymmetry crossings, and crossings can also appear away from the GOE reference. A near-staggered detuned control further shows that even an inversion of the total charge-sector coherence need not produce an entanglement-asymmetry crossing. Thus the crossing response is controlled not by spectral chaos alone, but by how local charge-sector coherence enters the reduced density matrix.

motivation: The quantum Mpemba effect is a counterintuitive phenomenon where a state with stronger symmetry breaking can restore symmetry faster. Understanding its underlying mechanisms is important for non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors numerically study a clean U(1)-conserving spin chain with various field textures, comparing spectral level statistics (GOE-like vs. non-GOE) with entanglement asymmetry crossings. They also analyze a near-staggered detuned control to probe the role of charge-sector coherence.
result: GOE-like level statistics do not guarantee Mpemba crossings; crossings can occur even without GOE spectra, and vice versa. The crossing response is governed by local charge-sector coherence in the reduced density matrix, not by spectral chaos.
conclusion: Spectral chaos is not the decisive factor for quantum Mpemba crossings; instead, the local structure of charge-sector coherence plays a key role, highlighting the need for more refined thermodynamic indicators.

title: Feynman's Clock And Hierarchy-informed Sampling For Quantum Error Mitigation
authors: Theo Saporiti
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Near-term physical implementations of quantum algorithms require efficient quantum error mitigation schemes to reduce quantum noise. In this letter we propose a new mitigation technique, by extending the applicability of our BBGKY-ISM scheme from quantum simulations of spin chains to arbitrary quantum circuits. We map executions of quantum circuits using Feynman's clock Hamiltonian to the Hamiltonian dynamics of a corresponding quantum system, whose time evolution obeys a BBGKY-like hierarchy of equations informing the BBGKY-ISM mitigation. We show that the method's classical and quantum overheads are polynomial in the circuit size and in the number of qubits. We apply our method to numerical simulations of tunable Bell state preparation circuits under state-of-the-art quantum noise, and numerically demonstrate its systematic and controllable quantum error reduction capability.

motivation: Near-term quantum devices suffer from noise, requiring efficient error mitigation techniques to improve computation fidelity.
method: Maps quantum circuit executions to Hamiltonian dynamics via Feynman's clock, then applies a BBGKY-like hierarchy to inform a mitigation scheme (BBGKY-ISM) with polynomial overhead.
result: Numerical simulations on Bell state preparation circuits under realistic noise demonstrate systematic and controllable error reduction.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a practical, scalable approach to quantum error mitigation for near-term quantum computing.

title: Spectral Born Machines: Classically Trainable Quantum Generative Models For Discrete Data
authors: Austin Huang, William Maxwell, Vasilis Belis, Evan Peters, Jason Pye, Soran Jahangiri, Joseph Bowles
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present , a class of quantum generative models that results from viewing and generalizing the class of IQP Born machines through the lens of group Fourier analysis. These quantum models exploit the quantum Fourier transform to create an inductive bias that make them naturally suited to learning integer-structured data, while remaining classically hard to sample from in general. Similar to IQP Born machines, spectral Born machines can be trained efficiently at scale on classical hardware via a maximum mean discrepancy loss based on graph spectral analysis, which we make available in a new module of the PennyLane software platform. In numerical experiments, we show how the spectral bias of the model leads to significantly reduced parameter counts compared to unstructured approaches, and demonstrate the scalability of the software by training a 190-qubit model with over 1 million parameters to successfully learn a distribution of 93 nucleotide-long ribosomal RNA. Our results suggest that highly over-parameterized spectral Born machines may be immune to overfitting, even in strongly data-scarce regimes.

title: Enhanced Two-photon Sources In A Cavity-coupled Two-atom System
authors: Zhicai Chen, Jun Xu, Deyi Kong, Xiangming Hu, Fei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a component-selective scheme for improving two-photon sources in a cavity-coupled two-atom system, where a single cavity mode interacts with two two-level atoms driven by phase-controlled classical fields of the same frequency. By controlling the atomic detunings and driving phase, the system can be tailored toward optimized cavity-field two-photon blockade or strongly correlated fluorescence photon-pair emission. When the two-cavity-photon component is enhanced, the cavity field exhibits optimized two-photon blockade with simultaneous suppression of unwanted one- and three-photon components at a comparable two-photon population. In another parameter regime, strongly correlated fluorescence photon pairs can also be generated from the two atoms by selecting the double-atomic-excitation component in the same two-excitation manifold. This approach provides a route toward high-quality and versatile two-photon sources, with potential applications in few-photon quantum optics and quantum information processing.

motivation: High-quality two-photon sources are crucial for quantum optics and quantum information processing, but existing sources have limitations in purity and brightness.
method: A cavity mode interacts with two driven two-level atoms; by tuning atomic detunings and driving phase, the system can be tailored for two-photon blockade or correlated photon-pair emission.
result: Optimized two-photon blockade with suppressed one- and three-photon components, and strongly correlated fluorescence photon pairs are achieved in different parameter regimes.
conclusion: The scheme provides a versatile route to high-quality two-photon sources for few-photon quantum optics and quantum information applications.

In the two-photon blockade regime, the cavity field exhibits enhanced two-photon population while suppressing unwanted one- and three-photon components. In the fluorescence regime, strongly correlated photon pairs are generated by selecting the double-atomic-excitation component within the same two-excitation manifold. The approach offers a versatile route to high-quality two-photon sources for applications in few-photon quantum optics and quantum information processing.

title: Phase-Selected Efficient Single-Photon Frequency Conversion Via Local Fano Resonance In A Two-Giant-Atom Waveguide-QED System
authors: Qing-Ao Xiang, Yan Liu, Xin-Yuan Yang, Ya-Ju Song
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient single-photon frequency conversion is investigated in a two-giant-atom waveguide-QED system, where a two-level giant atom and a [MATH]-type three-level giant atom couple to a common one-dimensional waveguide. While the [MATH]-type atom provides the inelastic channel, the two-level atom induces secondary coherent coupling, creating multi-path interference for the converted photon. Using the real-space approach and within the Markovian approximation, we derive analytical four-channel scattering amplitudes and reveal that the inelastic transmission spectrum, governed by three complex resonance poles, exhibits a multi-peak interference pattern. By introducing a local single-pole approximation, we reduce this complex spectrum to a local Fano lineshape, decomposing it into a coherent superposition of a local background term and a single-pole resonant term. The interplay between these two terms-controlled by the photon propagation phase between the giant atoms' coupling points-determines the conversion efficiency, with the background suppression condition leading to a Lorentzian reduction. Based on the single-pole resonance weight, we formulate a phase-selection criterion for highly efficient conversion. Compared with both the small-atom and single [MATH]-type giant-atom models, the two-giant-atom scheme achieves substantially enhanced inelastic transmission over a broader frequency-conversion range. This work reveals how phase-controlled local Fano resonance enables high-efficiency frequency conversion, establishing a general paradigm for engineering resonant light-matter interactions in structured quantum systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a two-giant-atom waveguide-QED system for efficient single-photon frequency conversion via phase-controlled local Fano resonance.
motivation: Efficient single-photon frequency conversion is crucial for quantum networks and hybrid quantum systems, but existing schemes suffer from limited efficiency and narrow bandwidth.
method: The authors use a real-space approach and Markovian approximation to derive analytical four-channel scattering amplitudes, and introduce a local single-pole approximation to reduce the complex spectrum to a Fano lineshape.
result: The two-giant-atom scheme achieves substantially enhanced inelastic transmission over a broader frequency-conversion range compared to small-atom and single giant-atom models, with a phase-selection criterion for high efficiency.
conclusion: Phase-controlled local Fano resonance enables high-efficiency frequency conversion, establishing a general paradigm for engineering resonant light-matter interactions in structured quantum systems.

The Λ-type atom provides an inelastic channel for frequency conversion, while the two-level atom introduces secondary coherent coupling, enabling multi-path interference for the converted photon. By introducing a local single-pole approximation, they reduce this complex spectrum to a local Fano lineshape, decomposing it into a coherent superposition of a local background term and a single-pole resonant term. The interplay between these terms, controlled by the photon propagation phase between the giant atoms' coupling points, determines the conversion efficiency. The background suppression condition leads to a Lorentzian reduction, and based on the single-pole resonance weight, a phase-selection criterion for highly efficient conversion is formulated. Compared with both the small-atom and single Λ-type giant-atom models, the two-giant-atom scheme achieves substantially enhanced inelastic transmission over a broader frequency-conversion range. They model the system under the Markovian approximation, which assumes a frequency-independent coupling strength and is valid when the atomic linewidth is much smaller than the bandwidth of the waveguide. The giant atoms are characterized by multiple coupling points to the waveguide, introducing a phase factor e^{iφ} that depends on the distance between coupling points. The scattering problem is solved by writing the wavefunction in real space and imposing boundary conditions at each coupling point, leading to a set of linear equations. title: Dynamical Structure Factor With A Pumping Approach On A Trapped-ion Quantum Computer
authors: Etienne Granet, Keisuke Murota, Henrik Dreyer, Kentaro Yamamoto, Juan Pedersen, Hidemaro Suwa
abstract: ArXiv:2607.07138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamical structure factors (DSF) measured with neutron-scattering experiments provide key insights into the structure of materials. Their computation requires both the preparation of an equilibrium state and the implementation of Hamiltonian dynamics. We demonstrate the feasibility of computing DSF on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer, comparing the DSF of 1D Heisenberg model on [MATH] sites, and that of the copper sulfate crystal. To that end, we introduce a pumping approach for computing the DSF [MATH] on quantum computers that enables targeting specific arbitrary values of frequencies [MATH]. This method time-evolves the initial state using a time-dependent Hamiltonian perturbed by a source term oscillating at the target frequency [MATH]. When targeting only a few frequency values, this approach provides a significant reduction in shot overhead compared to previous methods.
tldr: This paper demonstrates computing dynamical structure factors on a trapped-ion quantum computer using a pumping approach.
motivation: Dynamical structure factors are important for understanding material properties, but their computation on quantum computers is challenging due to the need for equilibrium state preparation and Hamiltonian dynamics.
method: The authors introduce a pumping approach that time-evolves the initial state with a time-dependent Hamiltonian perturbed by a source term oscillating at a target frequency, enabling efficient computation of DSF at specific frequencies.
result: They demonstrate the feasibility on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer for the 1D Heisenberg model and copper sulfate crystal, showing reduced shot overhead when targeting few frequencies.
conclusion: The pumping approach offers a practical method for computing DSF on near-term quantum computers, with potential applications in materials science.

The authors introduce a novel 'pumping approach' that computes DSF S(q,ω) by time-evolving an initial state under a time-dependent Hamiltonian with a source term oscillating at a target frequency ω. This method allows targeting specific frequency values, reducing shot overhead compared to previous methods when only a few frequencies are needed. The results show good agreement with classical simulations and experimental data, validating the approach for near-term quantum devices.

title: A Quantum Model For Synchronizing Finite State Transition Systems
authors: Martin Lukac, Khaled El-Fakih, Uraz Turker
abstract: ArXiv:2607.06953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a quantum model for finding a resetting input sequence (RS) which can take a finite state transition system (FA), to particular state independent of its current state.
